To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cytokines required for optimal clonogenic growth of progenitor cells mobilized into the blood of patients by chemotherapy and cytokines are stem cell factor, interleukin‐6, interleukin 3 and granulocytes colony stimulating factor, and that most of these progenitors are multipotential.

(1) CD34‐selection of progenitor cells from peripheral blood has little effect on their cytokine requirements; (2) erythroid progenitors can be stimulated by a single cytokine, IL‐3, but require a mixture of cytokines for optimal growth; (3) myeloid progenitors require a mixture of IL‐3, GM‐CSF and G‐CSF for optimal growth; and (4) most mobilized progenitor cells are multipotental.

(1) cytokines, particularly stem cell factor and interleukine‐3, can support considerable erythroid colony growth in both unselected and CD34+ cells suspensions; and (2) optimal colony growth of both erythroid and granulocyte monocytes progenitors, after CD34 seletion, requires the addition of cytokines in addition to erythropoietin.

The main takeaway from our work is that

cytokines, such as interleukin‐6 and granulocyte macrophage colony‐stimulating factor, are required for optimal growth of progenitor cells, but that the addition of a mixture of cytokines, including stem cell factor, is essential for maximal clonogenic growth, especially in CD34‐selected cells.

, although the cytokines are required to support the proliferation of the progenitor cells, the presence of accessory cells, which may be lost during CD34 selection is required for optimal growth of the progenitor cell population.
